description:
We are Heroicos en Órbita, a team of high school students from Tacna, Peru, passionate about technology, robotics, and innovation. We are excited to join the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge and develop creative solutions.

We chose The Earth Information Jukebox to make Earth science accessible to everyone. Our project transforms NASA's Earth visualizations into interactive sounds, helping people with visual impairments explore our planet independently and discover its environmental challenges.
summary:
Lydia Jukebox is an interactive web application that offers an immersive audio-visual and sensory experience designed to engage users with space exploration and Earth science. Developed as a dynamic educational platform, it invites users to explore four distinct features through sound-guided navigation and intuitive storytelling.

The project addresses the challenge of making complex space and scientific concepts accessible and engaging to a broad audience. By transforming open scientific data and space mission themes into an interactive, sensory-rich interface, it removes technical barriers and turns passive learning into an active, memorable discovery process.

This initiative is important because it fosters scientific curiosity, promotes STEM engagement, and democratizes access to space and environmental knowledge. By combining creative design with accessible technology, it empowers learners of all backgrounds to connect meaningfully with space science.
details:
LYDIA is a web application developed by Heroicos en Órbita for NASA Space Apps’ The Earth Information Jukebox challenge. It makes Earth science visualizations more accessible by translating visual changes into sound in real time. A spoken welcome introduces the project, and audio descriptions guide users through three experiences.

In Sensory Climate Globe, users point with their index finger in front of a webcam to explore a virtual globe and hear sounds associated with different environments. Climate Change Image Explorer reads the color at the point the user indicates and updates the sound as the finger moves or the video advances. Its demonstration shows sea surface currents and temperatures in the eastern Pacific Ocean. In Color-to-Music Library, users select a map or image, hear a spoken description, and then listen to a composition generated from its colors.

We built LYDIA with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The Canvas API reads pixel colors, MediaPipe Hand Landmarker tracks the index finger, and the Web Audio API generates sound. MP3 recordings provide spoken guidance. We designed the experience around clear instructions, distinct sounds, and equipment commonly available in classrooms, such as a webcam and speakers or headphones.

LYDIA’s creative contribution is turning a simple pointing gesture into a way to explore a changing visualization by ear. Our goal is to give blind and low-vision users another way to engage with Earth science and help students compare patterns in scientific visualizations through sound and sight. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wiP3aiZS2_JkDscKcZ8iHsDiVxc8ziGz/view?usp=sharing
